title: Memory Hierarchy and Locality
subtitle: Why computers use a ladder of memories and why it works.

references.title: Large and Fast: Exploiting Memory Hierarchy
references.topics: Introduction; memory technologies; the basics of caches (principle of locality, hits and misses)

objectives: Explain why one huge, fast memory cannot be built
Describe the levels from registers to disk: speed, capacity and cost
Define temporal and spatial locality and recognise them in code
Explain hits, misses, hit rate and the idea of a block
Show how locality makes a hierarchy look like one big, fast memory

steps.question: Why can't we simply buy one huge memory that is as fast as the processor?
clues: Faster memories **cost far more per bit**.
The trick is to keep **what you will need soon** in a small, fast memory.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: Fast, large and cheap: pick two

items: A bigger memory has longer wires and more to search, so it is **slower**
Faster technology needs more transistors per bit, so it **costs more** and uses more power
No single technology is fast, large and cheap at the same time

steps.why: The hierarchy combines technologies: a little very fast memory near the CPU and a lot of slower memory further away.
steps.real: All the figures are order-of-magnitude values; they change with every generation.

mistake.wrong: We could make main memory as fast as registers if we paid enough.
mistake.right: Size and distance alone make a huge memory slower, and the cost would be enormous.

explainAgain.beginner: Your desk holds a few papers you can reach instantly; the bookshelf holds more but takes longer; the library holds everything but takes a trip.

steps.question: A processor reads a register in under 1 ns and DRAM in about 50 ns. If every instruction had to wait for DRAM, what would happen?
options: The processor would spend most of its time waiting

reveal.text: The CPU could do tens of operations in the time one DRAM access takes, so it would mostly sit idle. That gap is what the hierarchy hides.

steps.result: Next: how a small fast memory can hide a slow big one.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: If money were no object, could we build a 16 GB memory that responds in 1 ns?
ideas: A larger memory means longer wires and more decoding, so even SRAM would slow down.
16 GB of SRAM would need enormous area and power.
Signals take real time to travel across a chip.
So the answer is no: physics, not only cost, limits it.

steps.question: Which is true about memory technologies?
options: Faster memory is usually smaller and costs more per bit
Registers are cheaper than disks per bit
steps.why: Speed, size and cost trade off against each other.
feedback: DRAM is far faster than disks.
Registers are the most expensive per bit.

steps.title: The memory hierarchy

blocks.text: Closer to the CPU: **faster, smaller, more expensive per bit**. Further away: **slower, larger, cheaper per bit**. Click each level to see its role.

steps.why: Each level holds a copy of the most useful part of the level below it.
steps.real: Your laptop has all of these: registers, several cache levels, DRAM and an SSD.

explainAgain.beginner: A ladder: the top rung is the quickest to reach but holds the least.

levels.name: Registers

levels.purpose: Values the CPU is using right now

levels.purpose: The most recently used instructions and data
levels.example: A core's private instruction and data caches

levels.name: L2 cache

levels.capacity: several MB to tens of MB

levels.name: Main memory (DRAM)
levels.purpose: All running programs and their data

steps.why: Notice the pattern as you click down: speed falls, capacity rises, cost per bit falls.

steps.title: Hit, miss, block

items: The CPU asks the top level first
**Hit**: the data is in that level; **miss**: it is not and the next level is asked
Data moves between levels in **blocks** (several neighbouring words), not one word at a time
**Hit rate** = hits ÷ accesses; **miss rate** = 1 − hit rate

terms.note: every access is one or the other
the unit copied between two levels

steps.why: Almost all accesses should be satisfied by the top few levels, so the slow levels are rarely used.
steps.real: A typical program hits L1 more than 95% of the time.

steps.title: Preview: the average access time

blocks.title: Average memory access time (preview of Class 19)
blocks.equation: Average time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty

results.label: Compared with going to memory every time

steps.why: With a 95% hit rate the average is 6 ns, about 17 times faster than using main memory for every access. At 90% it is 11 ns; at 99% only 2 ns.

steps.question: L1 takes 1 ns, main memory 100 ns, and 95% of accesses hit in L1. What is the average access time?

reveal.text: Average = 1 + 0.05 × 100 = **6 ns**: the few misses cost a lot but are rare.

steps.result: We study this formula in Class 19.

steps.title: The principle of locality

head: Type
Meaning
Example
rows: A location used now is likely to be used again soon
A loop counter or a sum variable used every iteration
Locations near a used one are likely to be used soon
Walking through an array element by element

steps.why: Programs are not random: they loop and walk through data. Locality is what makes a small cache so effective.
steps.real: Instructions have locality too: the loop body is fetched thousands of times.

mistake.wrong: Locality is a property of the hardware.
mistake.right: It is a property of programs; the hardware exploits it.

explainAgain.beginner: If you read a page of a book you will probably read the next page too (spatial) and probably reread this page (temporal).

steps.question: In the loop above, which variables show temporal locality and which data shows spatial locality?
options: sum and i: temporal; array[i]: spatial

reveal.text: **sum** and **i** are touched on every iteration (temporal). **array[0], array[1], array[2]...** are neighbours in memory and are read one after another (spatial).

steps.result: The same loop shows both kinds at once.

steps.title: How the hierarchy exploits locality

items: **Temporal**: keep recently used data in the fast levels
**Spatial**: when one word is fetched, copy its whole **block** (neighbours) up as well
After one miss, the next few accesses in the same block are hits
Data that is never reused or scattered gets little benefit

steps.why: Blocks turn spatial locality into hits; keeping data turns temporal locality into hits.
steps.real: This is why walking an array row by row is much faster than jumping around.

steps.title: Try it: three access patterns

locality.title: Where is each word found?
locality.hint: Choose a pattern and press Step: **Found at** says which level supplied the word. Blocks hold 4 words; L1 holds 2 blocks and L2 holds 8.

steps.why: Nearby: 3 misses to memory, 9 L1 hits (one miss, then 3 hits per block). Repeated: 1 miss, 7 hits. Scattered: no L1 hits at all.

steps.question: Walking through words 0 to 11 with 4-word blocks: how many of the 12 accesses must go all the way to main memory?

reveal.text: The first word of each block (0, 4 and 8) misses and brings its whole block; the other three words of each block are then found in L1: **3 misses, 9 hits**.

steps.result: The block size turns one miss into several hits.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about locality is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. Temporal locality means reusing a recently used location.
2. Spatial locality means using locations near a recently used one.
3. Random scattered accesses have a lot of spatial locality.
4. A loop counter shows temporal locality.
steps.explain: Scattered accesses are far apart, so they show little spatial locality.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: Which has better locality: summing a 2D array row by row or column by column (the array is stored row by row)?
steps.answer: Row by row has good spatial locality: consecutive accesses are neighbours in memory, so each block fetched serves several accesses. Column by column jumps by a whole row each time, so each access may need a new block: many more misses.

questions.a: A location used recently is likely to be used again soon.
Locations near a used one are likely to be used soon.
They bring neighbouring words up together, so later accesses hit.

steps.title: A first look at a cache

blocks.text: A **cache** is a small, fast memory holding copies of recently used blocks. Class 18 explains exactly how it finds them. For now, watch hits and misses under different access patterns and block sizes.

steps.why: A larger block exploits spatial locality; reuse exploits temporal locality; scattered accesses defeat both.
steps.real: This is the same machinery in L1, L2 and L3.

steps.title: Try it: a small cache

blocks.title: Cache first look
blocks.hint: Switch the **block size** between 4 and 16 bytes and compare the sequential pattern.

steps.why: Sequential with 16-byte blocks: 6 hits of 8 (75%). With 4-byte blocks: 0 hits. Repeating one word: 7 of 8. Scattered: 0 of 8.

steps.question: The same eight sequential word addresses with 16-byte blocks give 6 hits. How many hits with 4-byte blocks?

reveal.text: With 4-byte blocks each word is its own block, so every access is a first touch: **0 hits**. The bigger block brought the neighbours along.

steps.result: Block size is how spatial locality becomes hits.

steps.question: Which access pattern benefits from a cache the least?
options: A loop over a small array
steps.why: There is neither reuse nor neighbours to exploit.
feedback: A small loop reuses the array.

steps.statement: A miss means the data was not in the level that was asked.
steps.why: The request goes to the next level down.

steps.question: List the memory hierarchy from fastest to slowest.
steps.answer: Registers, L1 cache, L2 and L3 caches, main memory (DRAM), SSD / HDD.
steps.solution: Speed falls and capacity rises as you go down.

steps.question: In `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) total += data[i];` name the locality shown by `total` and by `data[i]`.
steps.answer: `total` shows temporal locality; `data[i]` shows spatial locality.
steps.solution: total is reused every iteration; data[i] is read in order.
steps.hint: Is the location reused, or are neighbours used?

steps.question: Words 0 to 11 are read with 4-word blocks. How many accesses miss to main memory, and what is the L1 hit rate?
steps.solution: Words 0, 4 and 8 start new blocks. The other nine words are in blocks already copied.
steps.hint: Count how many words each block serves.
steps.mistake: Counting every access as a miss.

steps.question: L1 takes 1 ns, main memory 100 ns. Find the average access time when the L1 hit rate is (a) 90%, (b) 95%, (c) 99%.
steps.mistake: Using the hit rate instead of the miss rate.
steps.title: Exam practice: calculation

steps.question: With 4-word blocks, L1 of 2 blocks and L2 of 8 blocks, the pattern 3, 90, 41, 17, 64, 2, 77, 30 is read. How many words are found in L1, in L2 and in main memory?
steps.answer: 0 in L1, 1 in L2 (word 2, in block 0 already copied by word 3) and 7 in main memory.
steps.solution: All eight words are in different blocks except 3 and 2 (both block 0). L1 holds only 2 blocks, so block 0 has been evicted by the time word 2 is read, but L2 still has it.
steps.mistake: Expecting L1 hits for a scattered pattern.
steps.title: Exam practice: pattern analysis

steps.question: Compare the hit rates of reading 8 consecutive words, one word repeated 8 times, and 8 scattered words, with a cache of 16-byte blocks (4 lines).
steps.answer: Consecutive: 6 of 8 (75%); repeated: 7 of 8 (87.5%); scattered: 0 of 8.
steps.solution: Consecutive words share 16-byte blocks (one miss per block); the repeated word misses once; the scattered words are all in different blocks.
steps.mistake: Thinking scattered accesses can hit by luck.
steps.title: Exam practice: comparison

steps.question: Explain why computers use a memory hierarchy instead of one large fast memory, and why the hierarchy works.
steps.answer: A memory that is large and fast does not exist: larger memories are slower, and fast technologies cost more per bit and use more power. A hierarchy keeps a small, fast memory next to the CPU and larger, slower memories behind it. It works because programs show locality: they reuse recent data (temporal) and use nearby data (spatial), so most accesses are satisfied by the fast levels.
steps.solution: A strong answer mentions size, speed and cost, and both kinds of locality.
steps.mistake: Saying the hierarchy works because the slow memory is made faster.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: Fast memory is small and costly; large memory is slow and cheap: no single memory is all three.
The hierarchy: registers, L1, L2, L3, DRAM, SSD/HDD; closer to the CPU is faster and smaller.
Temporal locality: reuse of recent data. Spatial locality: use of nearby data.
Data moves in blocks; a hit is found in a level, a miss goes to the next level.
Average access time = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty.
Locality is a property of programs that the hierarchy exploits.

mistakes.wrong: One big fast memory is just expensive.
mistakes.right: Size and distance also make it slower.
It is a property of programs.
They have little locality, so they mostly miss.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: No single memory is fast, large and cheap, so computers use a hierarchy: a small fast memory near the CPU and larger slower ones behind it. Because programs show temporal and spatial locality, most accesses hit in the fast levels, and blocks bring neighbouring words up together. The average access time stays close to the fast level's time.
